Glare, sky glow, flora, and fauna are all significantly impacted by the presence of lighting. Changing an environment from having cycles of day and night to a mostly lighted environment will have significant impacts on the species within the space. 2.2.3.1 Glare There are two forms of glare: disability glare and discomfort glare. Disability glare negatively affects visual performance. It is caused by light scattering in the ocular media. This scattering of light in the eyes of the observer reduces the contrast of the object, thereby affecting visual performance. Disability glare is affected by the illuminance measured at the eye, distance from the glare source, and the background luminance. Research has shown that disability glare is not majorly influenced by the spectral power distribution of the glare source (Davoudian et al., 2014; Niedling et al., 2015; Wooten & Geri, 1987). Thus, roadway lighting from LED sources will have the same effect on disability glare as any other conventional roadway lighting source. Discomfort glare causes a sensation of annoyance or pain in the eyes of the observer. It is more psychological than physiological, and it is not as well understood as the disability glare. Like disability glare, it is also affected by illuminance measured at the eye, and the distance and the angle between the glare source and the observer and the background luminance. Spectral power distribution of the light source could affect discomfort glare perception, with light sources that have higher blue content or shorter wavelengths causing higher discomfort glare (Bullough et al., 2003). However, this study only evaluated glare from headlamps and not from overhead roadway lighting. For overhead lighting. some of the recent research also reported that LEDs with higher CCTs also resulted in higher discomfort glare (Huang et al., 2018). 23 However, these results also show that discomfort glare from LEDs could be a result of non- uniformity of the light sources and the CCT. Recent research has established the link between non-uniformity of the LED light source and discomfort glare (van Bommel, 2014). Ma et al. (2017) measured discomfort glare from LED sources of eight non-uniform patterns and showed that discomfort glare increased with increasing non-uniformity. Yang et al. (2017) also evaluated the effect of non-uniformity of the luminaries (raw LEDs [just LED matrices] vs. diffused LEDs) and showed that diffused LED sources have lower discomfort glare than raw LEDs for the same intensity. Research has shown that this non-uniform luminance distribution results in higher discomfort glare rating (Tashiro et al., 2015). Therefore, discomfort glare from LED sources is a result of optical design of the luminaires rather than the spectral power distribution. These research results show that there is lack of converging lines of evidence on the effects of the CCT of LEDs on discomfort glare. More research is required to definitively show that there is a link between CCT of the light source and discomfort glare. 2.2.3.2 Sky Glow There
